When the shopkeeper, an old man with a white beard that looked like it had caught bits of starlight, knelt down to wind its mechanism, the crank turned with a soft, rhythmic "click-clack" that sounded like a clock counting down to a memory. Then the needle dropped, a faint scrape against vinyl that made Lin Mian’s breath hitch, and a scratchy melody spilled out—Chen Yixun’s "Red Rose." It hit her like a wave breaking over a quiet shore; that was the exact song playing on the kitchen radio the morning her parents dragged their suitcases out the door, laughing as her mother tucked a strand of hair behind her ear and promised to bring back a silk scarf from Suzhou. She’d stood in the doorway, clutching her favorite teddy bear, watching their car vanish around the maple tree at the end of the lane, never guessing it would be the last time she’d see their smiles.

Her breath caught in her throat, and she reached out unconsciously to touch the cold metal needle, its tip glinting like a tiny diamond under the shop’s dim incandescent bulb. Just as her fingertip brushed the tiny lever that controlled the arm, it collided with another hand. Warm, calloused from turning camera knobs and tightening screws, with a faint silvery scar along the knuckle—like a line drawn by a careless needle during a childhood mishap. Lin Mian jerked back as if burned, her cheeks flushing pink as the cherry blossoms that fell in spring, and when she looked up, she met a pair of amber eyes, crinkled at the corners like someone who smiled often, even when alone with a stack of old records. His lashes were thick, casting soft shadows in the low light, and there was a hint of amusement in his gaze—not at her awkwardness, but at the way their hands had tangled so naturally, as if they’d been reaching for the same thing all along.

"Sorry," the man said, pulling his hand back slightly—not in retreat, but in the quiet courtesy of someone who respected personal space. He was wearing a well-worn denim jacket, the cuffs rolled up to reveal a faded blue watch with a cracked glass face; its hands still ticked steadily, though the numbers were half-rubbed off, a testament to years of reliable service. "I’ve been coming to check on this thing for a month. The old man here says it’s a 1992 model, from a family that moved abroad to Canada. Works like a charm if you’re gentle with the needle—she’s a bit temperamental, like an old lady who doesn’t suffer fools." He nodded at the phonograph, his tone fond, as if speaking of an old friend who’d shared countless mornings and evenings with him. "I almost missed it last week—he was gonna sell it to a collector from Shanghai, but I begged him to hold on. Told him it wasn’t just a machine to me."

Lin Mian nodded, her throat suddenly dry as cotton left in the sun. She’d wandered into the bookstore twenty minutes earlier to escape the sudden late-autumn downpour—those southern city rains that came out of nowhere, drumming on the awning like a thousand fingertips and turning the sidewalks into glossy mirrors that reflected the streetlights. The damp had seeped into her canvas shoes, making her toes cold, and her hair clung in soft ringlets to her neck, leaving cool little patches on her skin that sent a shiver through her. The man glanced at the rain streaking the fogged windows, then back at her, his gaze lingering on the way she hugged her arms around her chest, as if trying to ward off a chill that wasn’t just from the weather, but from the empty spaces in her life.

"Want a cup of hot cocoa?" He tilted his chin toward the small counter by the door, where a chipped enamel kettle whistled softly, sending a wisp of steam curling toward the ceiling like a lazy question. "The shopkeeper makes it with real milk and a pinch of cinnamon—tastes like my grandma’s, back when she still had all her teeth and could bake osmanthus cakes that filled the whole alley with sweetness. I owed him a favor for holding the phonograph for me; he’s been letting me store a few of my camera boxes in the back room, so this is the least I can do." There was a boyish grin in his voice, the kind that made even the dust motes dancing in the light seem friendlier, and Lin Mian found herself nodding before she could overthink the kindness of a stranger. Something about him—his warm eyes, the way he spoke of his grandma, the reverence in his voice when he talked about the phonograph—made her feel safe, a feeling she hadn’t known since her parents left.

His name was Jiang Chen. He repaired old cameras for a living, working out of a tiny studio two blocks west, above a noodle shop that smelled like garlic and sesame oil all day long—so much so that his clothes always carried a faint, comforting aroma of home-cooked food. Over steaming mugs of cocoa—rich, sweet, and warm enough to seep into her bones and chase away the last of the rain’s chill—he told her he collected vintage audio equipment because his grandfather had been a radio repairman back in the 70s. "Grandpa’s shop was in the old town, by the river," he said, wiping a drop of cocoa from his lower lip with the back of his hand. "Wooden shelves lined with resistors and capacitors, a faded poster of Teresa Teng on the wall, and this exact phonograph by the door. He’d play ‘The Moon Represents My Heart’ every single morning while he polished his soldering iron—like a ritual, y’know? Even when his hands started to shake, he’d still wind it up. When he passed, the shop got torn down for a mall, but I’ve been looking for something to remind me of him ever since. Something that wasn’t just a tool, but a piece of him."

Lin Mian told him she was a primary school art teacher, that she loved watercolors because they blended softly, no harsh lines—like memories that fade around the edges but never truly disappear, their colors seeping into the corners of your mind. She didn’t mention the empty house she’d moved back into after the accident, the way she still set three bowls at dinner sometimes (reaching for a third pair of chopsticks before the cold weight of loss settled in), or how she’d started sleeping with her mom’s old sweater tucked under her pillow. But when Jiang Chen talked about his grandfather’s hands—gnarled from years of twisting screws, but steady enough to thread a wire through a tiny hole—the words spilled out, unplanned and raw. "My dad fixed things too," she said, staring at her cocoa, watching the steam curl into little clouds. "He built a treehouse for me when I was seven, in the oak tree in our backyard. It took him three weekends; he pricked his thumb so many times I thought he’d bleed out. I made him a band-aid out of construction paper and glitter—pink, his least favorite color—and he wore it to work every day that week. His coworkers teased him, but he just said it was his ‘lucky charm.’" Her voice softened, and she smiled at the memory, the first genuine one that hadn’t tasted like sadness in weeks.

Jiang Chen laughed, a warm sound that made the cold shop feel brighter. "My grandpa once tried to fix a record player with a rubber band. It played ‘Moon River’ at double speed for a week. We couldn’t stop laughing whenever it came on."

The rain stopped at dusk. Jiang Chen walked her to the bus stop, and before she got on, he said, "I’m gonna buy that phonograph tomorrow. If you want… you could come over sometime. I’ve got a stack of old records my grandpa left me. Teresa Teng, Zhou Xuan, even some old jazz."

Lin Mian nodded before she could overthink it. She wrote her phone number on a scrap of paper from her sketchbook—there was a tiny watercolor of a cat in the corner—and handed it to him. His fingers brushed hers again, and this time, she didn’t pull away.

Jiang Chen’s studio was on the third floor of an old brick building, with a skylight that let in soft light during the day. The walls were lined with shelves holding cameras of every shape and size—boxy Polaroids from the 80s, sleek rangefinders from the 60s, a wooden view camera that looked like it belonged in a museum. The phonograph sat on a wooden table by the window, its horn polished to a faint shine. Next to it was a stack of records, their sleeves slightly faded.

"I cleaned it up yesterday," Jiang Chen said, winding the crank. "Want to pick a record?"

Lin Mian ran her finger along the spines. She stopped at a yellowed sleeve with a black-and-white photo of a woman in a cheongsam, holding a microphone. "Teresa Teng?"

"My grandpa’s favorite," he said. He took the record from her, placed it gently on the turntable, and dropped the needle. "The Moon Represents My Heart" filled the room, slow and sweet, like honey melting on toast. Lin Mian felt a sudden tightness in her chest—not the anxious kind, but the kind that comes when something feels exactly right.

Jiang Chen pulled out two folding chairs, and they sat there for an hour, listening to record after record. He told her about the time he’d traveled to Chengdu to buy a rare Rolleiflex, how he’d gotten lost in a market and ended up eating spicy hot pot with a group of elders. She told him about her students—Xiao Yu, who drew cats on every worksheet; Xiao Hong, who was afraid of watercolors but loved oil pastels; the time the whole class had painted a mural of the city’s old streets on the school wall.

When she left, it was dark outside. Jiang Chen walked her down the stairs, and at the door, he said, "I made something for you." He handed her a small envelope. Inside was a polaroid photo—of the phonograph, with the sunset streaming through the skylight behind it. On the back, he’d written: "For the girl who loves watercolors and old songs."

Lin Mian taped the photo to the fridge that night. Next to it was a photo of her parents, taken at the Great Wall when she was ten. For the first time in months, she didn’t feel like the house was too big, too quiet.

They started seeing each other regularly. Sometimes he’d come to her school during recess, bringing steamed buns from the shop down the street. The kids would crowd around him, asking about his cameras, and he’d let them hold the small point-and-shoots he kept in his bag. "Mr. Jiang is cooler than Spider-Man," Xiao Yu told Lin Mian one day, loud enough for Jiang Chen to hear. He laughed and ruffled the boy’s hair.

Sometimes she’d go to his studio after work, bringing takeout—braised pork ribs from the restaurant his grandfather used to frequent, stir-fried greens from the market. She’d sit on the floor and watch him work, his brow furrowed as he adjusted a tiny screw with a pair of tweezers. "You’re very focused," she’d say, and he’d look up, his eyes softening. "Hard not to be when you’re here."

One weekend, he took her to the old town by the river. They walked along the stone streets, stopping at a tailor’s shop where his grandmother had bought clothes, a tea house where his grandfather had played chess. "I used to come here every summer when I was a kid," he said. "My grandma would give me five yuan to buy sugar-fried chestnuts, and I’d sit on the bridge and watch the boats go by."

They bought chestnuts from a street vendor, still warm in a paper bag, and sat on the bridge. The river glinted in the sunlight, and a group of children chased each other along the bank, laughing. Lin Mian leaned her head on his shoulder, and he wrapped his arm around her. "You know," he said, "my grandpa used to say that the best things in life are the ones that take time—fixing a camera, brewing good tea, loving someone."

Lin Mian squeezed his hand. "My mom used to say the same thing. She said love is like a watercolor painting. You start with light strokes, and then you build it up, layer by layer, until it’s something beautiful."

That night, they went back to his studio. He put on a record—"When I Fall in Love" by Nat King Cole—and pulled her close. They danced slowly, the phonograph’s melody mixing with the sound of the wind outside. Lin Mian closed her eyes, breathing in the scent of his soap and the faint smell of camera oil. For a moment, she forgot about the empty house, about the accident, about all the days she’d spent feeling like a part of her was missing. All she could feel was his hand on her back, his heartbeat against her chest, the warmth of his breath on her forehead.

Winter came, and with it, the anniversary of her parents’ death. Lin Mian woke up that morning with a heavy heart, the kind that made even getting out of bed feel like a chore. She stared at the ceiling for a long time, then got up and put on the sweater her mom had knitted for her—soft wool, light blue, a little too small now but still warm.

She was making coffee when the doorbell rang. It was Jiang Chen, holding a bouquet of white chrysanthemums and a paper bag. "I asked the shopkeeper about the best flowers for remembrance," he said, handing her the bouquet. "He said these are for people you love who are gone."

Lin Mian’s throat tightened. She’d never told him the exact date—she’d only mentioned that the anniversary was in December. He must have remembered, must have asked her neighbors or the school secretary. She stepped aside to let him in, and he put the flowers in a vase on the dining table, next to the photo of her parents.

"I made congee," he said, opening the paper bag. "My grandma used to make it when someone was sad. It’s plain, but it’s warm."

They sat at the table and ate congee slowly. Lin Mian told him about the last day she’d spent with her parents—they’d gone to the zoo, her dad had bought her a cotton candy that stained her fingers pink, her mom had taken a photo of her laughing with a giraffe. "I thought we’d have so many more days like that," she said, her voice breaking. "I was mad at them for a long time. For leaving me."

Jiang Chen took her hand, his thumb brushing over her knuckles. "It’s okay to be mad," he said. "Grief isn’t neat. My grandpa died when I was 16. I didn’t talk to anyone for a month. I thought if I didn’t, it wouldn’t be real." He paused. "But then I found his old toolbox, and all the notes he’d written about fixing cameras. It was like he was still there, teaching me things. Grief fades, but the love… that stays."

That afternoon, they took the chrysanthemums to the cemetery. Lin Mian placed the flowers on her parents’ grave, and Jiang Chen stood beside her, quiet, respectful. She told her parents about Jiang Chen—about his studio, his love for old cameras, the way he made her laugh when she was sad. "I think you’d like him," she said, brushing a leaf off the headstone. "He’s kind. Like you."

On the way back, it started snowing—light, flaky snow that melted as soon as it hit the ground. Jiang Chen held her hand, and they walked slowly, watching the snow fall. "You know what I love about snow?" he said. "It covers everything, but it doesn’t erase it. It just gives it a fresh start."

Lin Mian smiled. "My dad used to say that too. He said snow is nature’s way of saying ‘let’s try again.’"

That night, they went to his studio. He’d set up a blanket by the phonograph, with a plate of sugar-fried chestnuts and a thermos of hot tea. He put on a record—"Memory" by Barbara Streisand—and they sat together, watching the snow fall through the skylight. "I have something for you," he said, reaching into his pocket. He pulled out a small box, and when Lin Mian opened it, she gasped.

It was a silver locket, with a tiny camera engraved on the front. Inside was a polaroid photo—of her, painting by the river, the one he’d taken a month ago without her noticing. "My grandma had a locket like this," he said. "She kept a photo of my grandpa in it. I wanted you to have something to keep the people you love close."

Lin Mian put the locket around her neck. It was warm against her skin, like a hug. She leaned over and kissed him, soft at first, then deeper. When she pulled away, he was smiling, his eyes shining. "I love you," he said, quiet but sure. "I’ve loved you since the day we both reached for that phonograph."

"I love you too," she said. And for the first time, the words didn’t feel scary. They felt like coming home.

Spring came, and the old bookstore on Xingfu Road closed down. The shopkeeper gave Jiang Chen the phonograph as a gift, saying, "It’s better with someone who loves it." They moved it to Lin Mian’s house, placing it in the living room by the window, where the sunlight hit it just right.

Jiang Chen proposed that summer, on the bridge by the old town. He got down on one knee, holding a ring with a small diamond—"my grandma’s," he said—and asked her to marry him. The children from her class were hiding behind a tree, and when she said yes, they ran out, cheering, holding up signs that said "Mr. Jiang, marry our teacher!" Xiao Yu gave her a drawing of a cat wearing a wedding veil, and Jiang Chen laughed until his eyes watered.

They got married in the autumn, in the school’s backyard, where the maple trees were red and gold. Lin Mian wore a white dress, and Jiang Chen wore a suit that fit him perfectly—tailored by the same tailor his grandmother had used. The phonograph played "The Moon Represents My Heart" as she walked down the aisle, her dad’s old watch on her wrist, the locket around her neck. Her students sat in the front row, waving paper flowers they’d made themselves. The shopkeeper from the old bookstore was there, and the vendor who sold sugar-fried chestnuts, and Jiang Chen’s aunt, who’d traveled all the way from Beijing.

After the ceremony, they danced to "Red Rose," the song that had been playing the day they met. Jiang Chen held her close, and she rested her head on his shoulder, listening to the phonograph’s scratchy melody. "You know," she said, "my parents would have loved this."

"I know," he said, kissing the top of her head. "And my grandpa would have loved that we’re dancing to his phonograph."

That night, they moved into a new house—bigger than her old one, with a studio for Jiang Chen and a sunroom for Lin Mian to paint in. The phonograph sat in the living room, between a bookshelf filled with her watercolor supplies and a table where Jiang Chen repaired cameras. Every morning, Jiang Chen would wind it up and play a record—Teresa Teng, Nat King Cole, sometimes even the old jazz records his grandpa had loved. And every morning, Lin Mian would stand beside him, watching the needle move, feeling the warmth of his hand in hers.

A year later, Lin Mian found out she was pregnant. She told Jiang Chen while they were sitting by the phonograph, listening to "L-O-V-E" by Nat King Cole. He froze for a moment, then picked her up and spun her around, laughing so hard he almost knocked over the stack of records. That night, he took a polaroid of her hand resting on her stomach, and they put it in the locket next to the photo of her painting by the river.

Their daughter was born in the spring, a tiny girl with Jiang Chen’s amber eyes and Lin Mian’s curly hair. They named her Xiao Yue—Little Moon, after the song that had played on their first date. Every night, they’d put her in her crib and wind up the phonograph, letting the soft melody lull her to sleep. Jiang Chen would hold Lin Mian’s hand, and they’d watch their daughter sleep, listening to the scratchy music, feeling the quiet joy of a life built on love.

One afternoon, when Xiao Yue was three, she climbed onto a chair and reached for the phonograph, her tiny fingers brushing the brass horn. "Daddy, what’s this?" she asked, looking up at Jiang Chen with wide eyes.

Jiang Chen picked her up and sat her on his lap, winding the crank. "This is a phonograph," he said. "It plays old songs. Grandpa Jiang used to have one just like it." He dropped the needle, and "The Moon Represents My Heart" filled the room. Xiao Yue’s eyes lit up, and she started bouncing on his lap, clapping her hands.

Lin Mian stood in the doorway, watching them. She was holding a watercolor painting she’d just finished—of the phonograph, with Xiao Yue sitting on Jiang Chen’s lap, the sunlight streaming through the window. The locket hung around her neck, warm against her skin. She thought about the day she’d first seen the phonograph, about the rain, about the man with amber eyes who’d offered her a cup of hot cocoa. She thought about her parents, about Jiang Chen’s grandpa, about all the love that had been passed down from one generation to the next.

Jiang Chen looked up and saw her, and he smiled. He held out his hand, and she walked over, sitting down next to him. Xiao Yue climbed into her lap, wrapping her arms around her neck. "Mommy, sing!" she said, pointing at the phonograph.

Lin Mian started singing, her voice soft and clear. Jiang Chen joined in, and Xiao Yue babbled along, her tiny voice mixing with theirs. The phonograph played on, the needle moving slowly across the record, the melody filling the room with warmth.

Outside, the sun was shining, and the cherry blossoms were falling, pink petals drifting like snow. Inside, there was love—warm, steady, enduring—like the scratchy music from the old phonograph, like the watercolor paintings on the walls, like the handprints of a little girl on the windowsill. It was the kind of love that takes time, that builds layer by layer, that stays even when the days are hard. It was the kind of love that makes a house a home, that makes a life feel full.

Lin Mian looked at Jiang Chen, at Xiao Yue, at the old phonograph playing its song. And she knew, with a certainty that filled her chest, that this was what happiness looked like.

"Mr. Jiang is cooler than Spider-Man," Xiao Yu told Lin Mian one day, loud enough for Jiang Chen to hear. He laughed and ruffled the boy’s hair.

Sometimes she’d go to his studio after work, bringing takeout—braised pork ribs from the restaurant his grandfather used to frequent, stir-fried greens from the market. She’d sit on the floor and watch him work, his brow furrowed as he adjusted a tiny screw with a pair of tweezers. "You’re very focused," she’d say, and he’d look up, his eyes softening. "Hard not to be when you’re here."

One weekend, he took her to the old town by the river. They walked along the stone streets, stopping at a tailor’s shop where his grandmother had bought clothes, a tea house where his grandfather had played chess. "I used to come here every summer when I was a kid," he said. "My grandma would give me five yuan to buy sugar-fried chestnuts, and I’d sit on the bridge and watch the boats go by."

They bought chestnuts from a street vendor, still warm in a paper bag, and sat on the bridge. The river glinted in the sunlight, and a group of children chased each other along the bank, laughing. Lin Mian leaned her head on his shoulder, and he wrapped his arm around her. "You know," he said, "my grandpa used to say that the best things in life are the ones that take time—fixing a camera, brewing good tea, loving someone."

Lin Mian squeezed his hand. "My mom used to say the same thing. She said love is like a watercolor painting. You start with light strokes, and then you build it up, layer by layer, until it’s something beautiful."

That night, they went back to his studio. He put on a record—"When I Fall in Love" by Nat King Cole—and pulled her close. They danced slowly, the phonograph’s melody mixing with the sound of the wind outside. Lin Mian closed her eyes, breathing in the scent of his soap and the faint smell of camera oil. For a moment, she forgot about the empty house, about the accident, about all the days she’d spent feeling like a part of her was missing. All she could feel was his hand on her back, his heartbeat against her chest, the warmth of his breath on her forehead.

Winter came, and with it, the anniversary of her parents’ death. Lin Mian woke up that morning with a heavy heart, the kind that made even getting out of bed feel like a chore. She stared at the ceiling for a long time, then got up and put on the sweater her mom had knitted for her—soft wool, light blue, a little too small now but still warm.

She was making coffee when the doorbell rang. It was Jiang Chen, holding a bouquet of white chrysanthemums and a paper bag. "I asked the shopkeeper about the best flowers for remembrance," he said, handing her the bouquet. "He said these are for people you love who are gone."

Lin Mian’s throat tightened. She’d never told him the exact date—she’d only mentioned that the anniversary was in December. He must have remembered, must have asked her neighbors or the school secretary. She stepped aside to let him in, and he put the flowers in a vase on the dining table, next to the photo of her parents.

"I made congee," he said, opening the paper bag. "My grandma used to make it when someone was sad. It’s plain, but it’s warm."

They sat at the table and ate congee slowly. Lin Mian told him about the last day she’d spent with her parents—they’d gone to the zoo, her dad had bought her a cotton candy that stained her fingers pink, her mom had taken a photo of her laughing with a giraffe. "I thought we’d have so many more days like that," she said, her voice breaking. "I was mad at them for a long time. For leaving me."

Jiang Chen took her hand, his thumb brushing over her knuckles. "It’s okay to be mad," he said. "Grief isn’t neat. My grandpa died when I was 16. I didn’t talk to anyone for a month. I thought if I didn’t, it wouldn’t be real." He paused. "But then I found his old toolbox, and all the notes he’d written about fixing cameras. It was like he was still there, teaching me things. Grief fades, but the love… that stays."

That afternoon, they took the chrysanthemums to the cemetery. Lin Mian placed the flowers on her parents’ grave, and Jiang Chen stood beside her, quiet, respectful. She told her parents about Jiang Chen—about his studio, his love for old cameras, the way he made her laugh when she was sad. "I think you’d like him," she said, brushing a leaf off the headstone. "He’s kind. Like you."

On the way back, it started snowing—light, flaky snow that melted as soon as it hit the ground. Jiang Chen held her hand, and they walked slowly, watching the snow fall. "You know what I love about snow?" he said. "It covers everything, but it doesn’t erase it. It just gives it a fresh start."

Lin Mian smiled. "My dad used to say that too. He said snow is nature’s way of saying ‘let’s try again.’"

That night, they went to his studio. He’d set up a blanket by the phonograph, with a plate of sugar-fried chestnuts and a thermos of hot tea. He put on a record—"Memory" by Barbara Streisand—and they sat together, watching the snow fall through the skylight. "I have something for you," he said, reaching into his pocket. He pulled out a small box, and when Lin Mian opened it, she gasped.

It was a silver locket, with a tiny camera engraved on the front. Inside was a polaroid photo—of her, painting by the river, the one he’d taken a month ago without her noticing. "My grandma had a locket like this," he said. "She kept a photo of my grandpa in it. I wanted you to have something to keep the people you love close."

Lin Mian put the locket around her neck. It was warm against her skin, like a hug. She leaned over and kissed him, soft at first, then deeper. When she pulled away, he was smiling, his eyes shining. "I love you," he said, quiet but sure. "I’ve loved you since the day we both reached for that phonograph."

"I love you too," she said. And for the first time, the words didn’t feel scary. They felt like coming home.

Spring came, and the old bookstore on Xingfu Road closed down. The shopkeeper gave Jiang Chen the phonograph as a gift, saying, "It’s better with someone who loves it." They moved it to Lin Mian’s house, placing it in the living room by the window, where the sunlight hit it just right.

Jiang Chen proposed that summer, on the bridge by the old town. He got down on one knee, holding a ring with a small diamond—"my grandma’s," he said—and asked her to marry him. The children from her class were hiding behind a tree, and when she said yes, they ran out, cheering, holding up signs that said "Mr. Jiang, marry our teacher!" Xiao Yu gave her a drawing of a cat wearing a wedding veil, and Jiang Chen laughed until his eyes watered.

They got married in the autumn, in the school’s backyard, where the maple trees were red and gold. Lin Mian wore a white dress, and Jiang Chen wore a suit that fit him perfectly—tailored by the same tailor his grandmother had used. The phonograph played "The Moon Represents My Heart" as she walked down the aisle, her dad’s old watch on her wrist, the locket around her neck. Her students sat in the front row, waving paper flowers they’d made themselves. The shopkeeper from the old bookstore was there, and the vendor who sold sugar-fried chestnuts, and Jiang Chen’s aunt, who’d traveled all the way from Beijing.

After the ceremony, they danced to "Red Rose," the song that had been playing the day they met. Jiang Chen held her close, and she rested her head on his shoulder, listening to the phonograph’s scratchy melody. "You know," she said, "my parents would have loved this."

"I know," he said, kissing the top of her head. "And my grandpa would have loved that we’re dancing to his phonograph."

That night, they moved into a new house—bigger than her old one, with a studio for Jiang Chen and a sunroom for Lin Mian to paint in. The phonograph sat in the living room, between a bookshelf filled with her watercolor supplies and a table where Jiang Chen repaired cameras. Every morning, Jiang Chen would wind it up and play a record—Teresa Teng, Nat King Cole, sometimes even the old jazz records his grandpa had loved. And every morning, Lin Mian would stand beside him, watching the needle move, feeling the warmth of his hand in hers.

A year later, Lin Mian found out she was pregnant. She told Jiang Chen while they were sitting by the phonograph, listening to "L-O-V-E" by Nat King Cole. He froze for a moment, then picked her up and spun her around, laughing so hard he almost knocked over the stack of records. That night, he took a polaroid of her hand resting on her stomach, and they put it in the locket next to the photo of her painting by the river.

Their daughter was born in the spring, a tiny girl with Jiang Chen’s amber eyes and Lin Mian’s curly hair. They named her Xiao Yue—Little Moon, after the song that had played on their first date. Every night, they’d put her in her crib and wind up the phonograph, letting the soft melody lull her to sleep. Jiang Chen would hold Lin Mian’s hand, and they’d watch their daughter sleep, listening to the scratchy music, feeling the quiet joy of a life built on love.

One afternoon, when Xiao Yue was three, she climbed onto a chair and reached for the phonograph, her tiny fingers brushing the brass horn. "Daddy, what’s this?" she asked, looking up at Jiang Chen with wide eyes.

Jiang Chen picked her up and sat her on his lap, winding the crank. "This is a phonograph," he said. "It plays old songs. Grandpa Jiang used to have one just like it." He dropped the needle, and "The Moon Represents My Heart" filled the room. Xiao Yue’s eyes lit up, and she started bouncing on his lap, clapping her hands.

Lin Mian stood in the doorway, watching them. She was holding a watercolor painting she’d just finished—of the phonograph, with Xiao Yue sitting on Jiang Chen’s lap, the sunlight streaming through the window. The locket hung around her neck, warm against her skin. She thought about the day she’d first seen the phonograph, about the rain, about the man with amber eyes who’d offered her a cup of hot cocoa. She thought about her parents, about Jiang Chen’s grandpa, about all the love that had been passed down from one generation to the next.

Jiang Chen looked up and saw her, and he smiled. He held out his hand, and she walked over, sitting down next to him. Xiao Yue climbed into her lap, wrapping her arms around her neck. "Mommy, sing!" she said, pointing at the phonograph.

Lin Mian started singing, her voice soft and clear. Jiang Chen joined in, and Xiao Yue babbled along, her tiny voice mixing with theirs. The phonograph played on, the needle moving slowly across the record, the melody filling the room with warmth.

Outside, the sun was shining, and the cherry blossoms were falling, pink petals drifting like snow. Inside, there was love—warm, steady, enduring—like the scratchy music from the old phonograph, like the watercolor paintings on the walls, like the handprints of a little girl on the windowsill. It was the kind of love that takes time, that builds layer by layer, that stays even when the days are hard. It was the kind of love that makes a house a home, that makes a life feel full.

Lin Mian looked at Jiang Chen, at Xiao Yue, at the old phonograph playing its song. And she knew, with a certainty that filled her chest, that this was what happiness looked like.

When the shopkeeper, an old man with a white beard that looked like it had caught bits of starlight, knelt down to wind its mechanism, the crank turned with a soft, rhythmic "click-clack" that sounded like a clock counting down to a memory. Then the needle dropped, a faint scrape against vinyl that made Lin Mian’s breath hitch, and a scratchy melody spilled out—Chen Yixun’s "Red Rose." It hit her like a wave breaking over a quiet shore; that was the exact song playing on the kitchen radio the morning her parents dragged their suitcases out the door, laughing as her mother tucked a strand of hair behind her ear and promised to bring back a silk scarf from Suzhou. She’d stood in the doorway, clutching her favorite teddy bear, watching their car vanish around the maple tree at the end of the lane, never guessing it would be the last time she’d see their smiles.

Her breath caught in her throat, and she reached out unconsciously to touch the cold metal needle, its tip glinting like a tiny diamond under the shop’s dim incandescent bulb. Just as her fingertip brushed the tiny lever that controlled the arm, it collided with another hand. "I’ve been coming to check on this thing for a month. The old man here says it’s a 1992 model, from a family that moved abroad to Canada. He nodded at the phonograph, his tone fond, as if speaking of an old friend who’d shared countless mornings and evenings with him. "I almost missed it last week—he was gonna sell it to a collector from Shanghai, but I begged him to hold on. Told him it wasn’t just a machine to me."

Lin Mian nodded, her throat suddenly dry as cotton left in the sun. She’d wandered into the bookstore twenty minutes earlier to escape the sudden late-autumn downpour—those southern city rains that came out of nowhere, drumming on the awning like a thousand fingertips and turning the sidewalks into glossy mirrors that reflected the streetlights. The damp had seeped into her canvas shoes, making her toes cold, and her hair clung in soft ringlets to her neck, leaving cool little patches on her skin that sent a shiver through her. The man glanced at the rain streaking the fogged windows, then back at her, his gaze lingering on the way she hugged her arms around her chest, as if trying to ward off a chill that wasn’t just from the weather, but from the empty spaces in her life.

"Want a cup of hot cocoa?" He tilted his chin toward the small counter by the door, where a chipped enamel kettle whistled softly, sending a wisp of steam curling toward the ceiling like a lazy question. "The shopkeeper makes it with real milk and a pinch of cinnamon—tastes like my grandma’s, back when she still had all her teeth and could bake osmanthus cakes that filled the whole alley with sweetness. His name was Jiang Chen. He repaired old cameras for a living, working out of a tiny studio two blocks west, above a noodle shop that smelled like garlic and sesame oil all day long—so much so that his clothes always carried a faint, comforting aroma of home-cooked food. Over steaming mugs of cocoa—rich, sweet, and warm enough to seep into her bones and chase away the last of the rain’s chill—he told her he collected vintage audio equipment because his grandfather had been a radio repairman back in the 70s. "Grandpa’s shop was in the old town, by the river," he said, wiping a drop of cocoa from his lower lip with the back of his hand. "Wooden shelves lined with resistors and capacitors, a faded poster of Teresa Teng on the wall, and this exact phonograph by the door. He’d play ‘The Moon Represents My Heart’ every single morning while he polished his soldering iron—like a ritual, y’know? Even when his hands started to shake, he’d still wind it up. When he passed, the shop got torn down for a mall, but I’ve been looking for something to remind me of him ever since. Something that wasn’t just a tool, but a piece of him."

Lin Mian told him she was a primary school art teacher, that she loved watercolors because they blended softly, no harsh lines—like memories that fade around the edges but never truly disappear, their colors seeping into the corners of your mind. She didn’t mention the empty house she’d moved back into after the accident, the way she still set three bowls at dinner sometimes (reaching for a third pair of chopsticks before the cold weight of loss settled in), or how she’d started sleeping with her mom’s old sweater tucked under her pillow. But when Jiang Chen talked about his grandfather’s hands—gnarled from years of twisting screws, but steady enough to thread a wire through a tiny hole—the words spilled out, unplanned and raw. It took him three weekends; he pricked his thumb so many times I thought he’d bleed out. I made him a band-aid out of construction paper and glitter—pink, his least favorite color—and he wore it to work every day that week. His coworkers teased him, but he just said it was his ‘lucky charm.’" Her voice softened, and she smiled at the memory, the first genuine one that hadn’t tasted like sadness in weeks.

Jiang Chen laughed, a warm sound that made the cold shop feel brighter. "My grandpa once tried to fix a record player with a rubber band. It played ‘Moon River’ at double speed for a week. We couldn’t stop laughing whenever it came on."

The rain stopped at dusk. Jiang Chen walked her to the bus stop, and before she got on, he said, "I’m gonna buy that phonograph tomorrow. If you want… you could come over sometime. I’ve got a stack of old records my grandpa left me. Teresa Teng, Zhou Xuan, even some old jazz."

Lin Mian nodded before she could overthink it. She wrote her phone number on a scrap of paper from her sketchbook—there was a tiny watercolor of a cat in the corner—and handed it to him. His fingers brushed hers again, and this time, she didn’t pull away.

The walls were lined with shelves holding cameras of every shape and size—boxy Polaroids from the 80s, sleek rangefinders from the 60s, a wooden view camera that looked like it belonged in a museum. When the shopkeeper, an old man with a white beard that looked like it had caught bits of starlight, knelt down to wind its mechanism, the crank turned with a soft, rhythmic "click-clack" that sounded like a clock counting down to a memory. Then the needle dropped, a faint scrape against vinyl that made Lin Mian’s breath hitch, and a scratchy melody spilled out—Chen Yixun’s "Red Rose." It hit her like a wave breaking over a quiet shore; that was the exact song playing on the kitchen radio the morning her parents dragged their suitcases out the door, laughing as her mother tucked a strand of hair behind her ear and promised to bring back a silk scarf from Suzhou. She’d stood in the doorway, clutching her favorite teddy bear, watching their car vanish around the maple tree at the end of the lane, never guessing it would be the last time she’d see their smiles.

Her breath caught in her throat, and she reached out unconsciously to touch the cold metal needle, its tip glinting like a tiny diamond under the shop’s dim incandescent bulb. Just as her fingertip brushed the tiny lever that controlled the arm, it collided with another hand. Warm, calloused from turning camera knobs and tightening screws, with a faint silvery scar along the knuckle—like a line drawn by a careless needle during a childhood mishap. Lin Mian jerked back as if burned, her cheeks flushing pink as the cherry blossoms that fell in spring, and when she looked up, she met a pair of amber eyes, crinkled at the corners like someone who smiled often, even when alone with a stack of old records. His lashes were thick, casting soft shadows in the low light, and there was a hint of amusement in his gaze—not at her awkwardness, but at the way their hands had tangled so naturally, as if they’d been reaching for the same thing all along.

"Sorry," the man said, pulling his hand back slightly—not in retreat, but in the quiet courtesy of someone who respected personal space. He was wearing a well-worn denim jacket, the cuffs rolled up to reveal a faded blue watch with a cracked glass face; its hands still ticked steadily, though the numbers were half-rubbed off, a testament to years of reliable service. "I’ve been coming to check on this thing for a month. The old man here says it’s a 1992 model, from a family that moved abroad to Canada. Works like a charm if you’re gentle with the needle—she’s a bit temperamental, like an old lady who doesn’t suffer fools." He nodded at the phonograph, his tone fond, as if speaking of an old friend who’d shared countless mornings and evenings with him. "I almost missed it last week—he was gonna sell it to a collector from Shanghai, but I begged him to hold on. Told him it wasn’t just a machine to me."

Lin Mian nodded, her throat suddenly dry as cotton left in the sun. The man glanced at the rain streaking the fogged windows, then back at her, his gaze lingering on the way she hugged her arms around her chest, as if trying to ward off a chill that wasn’t just from the weather, but from the empty spaces in her life.

Over steaming mugs of cocoa—rich, sweet, and warm enough to seep into her bones and chase away the last of the rain’s chill—he told her he collected vintage audio equipment because his grandfather had been a radio repairman back in the 70s. "Wooden shelves lined with resistors and capacitors, a faded poster of Teresa Teng on the wall, and this exact phonograph by the door. He’d play ‘The Moon Represents My Heart’ every single morning while he polished his soldering iron—like a ritual, y’know? Even when his hands started to shake, he’d still wind it up. When he passed, the shop got torn down for a mall, but I’ve been looking for something to remind me of him ever since. Something that wasn’t just a tool, but a piece of him."

She didn’t mention the empty house she’d moved back into after the accident, the way she still set three bowls at dinner sometimes (reaching for a third pair of chopsticks before the cold weight of loss settled in), or how she’d started sleeping with her mom’s old sweater tucked under her pillow. But when Jiang Chen talked about his grandfather’s hands—gnarled from years of twisting screws, but steady enough to thread a wire through a tiny hole—the words spilled out, unplanned and raw. It took him three weekends; he pricked his thumb so many times I thought he’d bleed out. I made him a band-aid out of construction paper and glitter—pink, his least favorite color—and he wore it to work every day that week. Lin Mian nodded before she could overthink it. She wrote her phone number on a scrap of paper from her sketchbook—there was a tiny watercolor of a cat in the corner—and handed it to him. His fingers brushed hers again, and this time, she didn’t pull away.

Jiang Chen’s studio was on the third floor of an old brick building, with a skylight that let in soft light during the day. The walls were lined with shelves holding cameras of every shape and size—boxy Polaroids from the 80s, sleek rangefinders from the 60s, a wooden view camera that looked like it belonged in a museum. She’d sit on the floor and watch him work, his brow furrowed as he adjusted a tiny screw with a pair of tweezers. "You’re very focused," she’d say, and he’d look up, his eyes softening. They walked along the stone streets, stopping at a tailor’s shop where his grandmother had bought clothes, a tea house where his grandfather had played chess. "You know," he said, "my grandpa used to say that the best things in life are the ones that take time—fixing a camera, brewing good tea, loving someone."

They danced slowly, the phonograph’s melody mixing with the sound of the wind outside. Lin Mian closed her eyes, breathing in the scent of his soap and the faint smell of camera oil. For a moment, she forgot about the empty house, about the accident, about all the days she’d spent feeling like a part of her was missing. All she could feel was his hand on her back, his heartbeat against her chest, the warmth of his breath on her forehead.

Winter came, and with it, the anniversary of her parents’ death. Lin Mian woke up that morning with a heavy heart, the kind that made even getting out of bed feel like a chore. She stared at the ceiling for a long time, then got up and put on the sweater her mom had knitted for her—soft wool, light blue, a little too small now but still warm.

She was making coffee when the doorbell rang. It was Jiang Chen, holding a bouquet of white chrysanthemums and a paper bag. "I asked the shopkeeper about the best flowers for remembrance," he said, handing her the bouquet. "He said these are for people you love who are gone."

Lin Mian’s throat tightened. She’d never told him the exact date—she’d only mentioned that the anniversary was in December. He must have remembered, must have asked her neighbors or the school secretary. She stepped aside to let him in, and he put the flowers in a vase on the dining table, next to the photo of her parents.

"I made congee," he said, opening the paper bag. "My grandma used to make it when someone was sad. It’s plain, but it’s warm."

They sat at the table and ate congee slowly. Lin Mian told him about the last day she’d spent with her parents—they’d gone to the zoo, her dad had bought her a cotton candy that stained her fingers pink, her mom had taken a photo of her laughing with a giraffe. "I thought we’d have so many more days like that," she said, her voice breaking. "I was mad at them for a long time. For leaving me."

Jiang Chen took her hand, his thumb brushing over her knuckles. "It’s okay to be mad," he said. "Grief isn’t neat. My grandpa died when I was 16. I didn’t talk to anyone for a month. I thought if I didn’t, it wouldn’t be real." He paused. "But then I found his old toolbox, and all the notes he’d written about fixing cameras. It was like he was still there, teaching me things. Grief fades, but the love… that stays."

That afternoon, they took the chrysanthemums to the cemetery. Lin Mian placed the flowers on her parents’ grave, and Jiang Chen stood beside her, quiet, respectful. She told her parents about Jiang Chen—about his studio, his love for old cameras, the way he made her laugh when she was sad. "I think you’d like him," she said, brushing a leaf off the headstone. "He’s kind. Like you."

On the way back, it started snowing—light, flaky snow that melted as soon as it hit the ground. Jiang Chen held her hand, and they walked slowly, watching the snow fall. "You know what I love about snow?" he said. "It covers everything, but it doesn’t erase it. It just gives it a fresh start."

Lin Mian smiled. "My dad used to say that too. He said snow is nature’s way of saying ‘let’s try again.’"

That night, they went to his studio. He’d set up a blanket by the phonograph, with a plate of sugar-fried chestnuts and a thermos of hot tea. He put on a record—"Memory" by Barbara Streisand—and they sat together, watching the snow fall through the skylight. "I have something for you," he said, reaching into his pocket. He pulled out a small box, and when Lin Mian opened it, she gasped.

"My grandma had a locket like this," he said. "She kept a photo of my grandpa in it. I wanted you to have something to keep the people you love close."

Lin Mian put the locket around her neck. It was warm against her skin, like a hug. She leaned over and kissed him, soft at first, then deeper. When she pulled away, he was smiling, his eyes shining. "I love you," he said, quiet but sure. "I’ve loved you since the day we both reached for that phonograph."

Jiang Chen would hold Lin Mian’s hand, and they’d watch their daughter sleep, listening to the scratchy music, feeling the quiet joy of a life built on love.

Jiang Chen picked her up and sat her on his lap, winding the crank. "This is a phonograph," he said. "It plays old songs. Grandpa Jiang used to have one just like it." The locket hung around her neck, warm against her skin. She thought about the day she’d first seen the phonograph, about the rain, about the man with amber eyes who’d offered her a cup of hot cocoa. She thought about her parents, about Jiang Chen’s grandpa, about all the love that had been passed down from one generation to the next.

Jiang Chen looked up and saw her, and he smiled. He held out his hand, and she walked over, sitting down next to him. Xiao Yue climbed into her lap, wrapping her arms around her neck. "Mommy, sing!" she said, pointing at the phonograph.

Lin Mian started singing, her voice soft and clear. Jiang Chen joined in, and Xiao Yue babbled along, her tiny voice mixing with theirs. The phonograph played on, the needle moving slowly across the record, the melody filling the room with warmth.

Outside, the sun was shining, and the cherry blossoms were falling, pink petals drifting like snow. Inside, there was love—warm, steady, enduring—like the scratchy music from the old phonograph, like the watercolor paintings on the walls, like the handprints of a little girl on the windowsill. It was the kind of love that takes time, that builds layer by layer, that stays even when the days are hard. It was the kind of love that makes a house a home, that makes a life feel full.

Lin Mian looked at Jiang Chen, at Xiao Yue, at the old phonograph playing its song. And she knew, with a certainty that filled her chest, that this was what happiness looked like.

But when Jiang Chen talked about his grandfather’s hands—gnarled from years of twisting screws, but steady enough to thread a wire through a tiny hole—the words spilled out, unplanned and raw. "My dad fixed things too," she said, staring at her cocoa, watching the steam curl into little clouds. "He built a treehouse for me when I was seven, in the oak tree in our backyard. It took him three weekends; he pricked his thumb so many times I thought he’d bleed out. I made him a band-aid out of construction paper and glitter—pink, his least favorite color—and he wore it to work every day that week. His coworkers teased him, but he just said it was his ‘lucky charm.’" Her voice softened, and she smiled at the memory, the first genuine one that hadn’t tasted like sadness in weeks.

Jiang Chen laughed, a warm sound that made the cold shop feel brighter. "My grandpa once tried to fix a record player with a rubber band. It played ‘Moon River’ at double speed for a week. We couldn’t stop laughing whenever it came on."

The rain stopped at dusk. Jiang Chen walked her to the bus stop, and before she got on, he said, "I’m gonna buy that phonograph tomorrow. If you want… you could come over sometime. I’ve got a stack of old records my grandpa left me. Teresa Teng, Zhou Xuan, even some old jazz."

Lin Mian nodded before she could overthink it. She wrote her phone number on a scrap of paper from her sketchbook—there was a tiny watercolor of a cat in the corner—and handed it to him. His fingers brushed hers again, and this time, she didn’t pull away.

Jiang Chen’s studio was on the third floor of an old brick building, with a skylight that let in soft light during the day. The walls were lined with shelves holding cameras of every shape and size—boxy Polaroids from the 80s, sleek rangefinders from the 60s, a wooden view camera that looked like it belonged in a museum. The phonograph sat on a wooden table by the window, its horn polished to a faint shine. Next to it was a stack of records, their sleeves slightly faded.

"I cleaned it up yesterday," Jiang Chen said, winding the crank. "Want to pick a record?"

Lin Mian ran her finger along the spines. She stopped at a yellowed sleeve with a black-and-white photo of a woman in a cheongsam, holding a microphone. "Teresa Teng?"

"My grandpa’s favorite," he said. He took the record from her, placed it gently on the turntable, and dropped the needle. "The Moon Represents My Heart" filled the room, slow and sweet, like honey melting on toast. Lin Mian felt a sudden tightness in her chest—not the anxious kind, but the kind that comes when something feels exactly right.

Jiang Chen pulled out two folding chairs, and they sat there for an hour, listening to record after record. He told her about the time he’d traveled to Chengdu to buy a rare Rolleiflex, how he’d gotten lost in a market and ended up eating spicy hot pot with a group of elders. She told him about her students—Xiao Yu, who drew cats on every worksheet; Xiao Hong, who was afraid of watercolors but loved oil pastels; the time the whole class had painted a mural of the city’s old streets on the school wall.

When she left, it was dark outside. Jiang Chen walked her down the stairs, and at the door, he said, "I made something for you." He handed her a small envelope. Inside was a polaroid photo—of the phonograph, with the sunset streaming through the skylight behind it. On the back, he’d written: "For the girl who loves watercolors and old songs."

Lin Mian taped the photo to the fridge that night. Next to it was a photo of her parents, taken at the Great Wall when she was ten. For the first time in months, she didn’t feel like the house was too big, too quiet.

They started seeing each other regularly. Sometimes he’d come to her school during recess, bringing steamed buns from the shop down the street. The kids would crowd around him, asking about his cameras, and he’d let them hold the small point-and-shoots he kept in his bag. "Mr. Jiang is cooler than Spider-Man," Xiao Yu told Lin Mian one day, loud enough for Jiang Chen to hear. He laughed and ruffled the boy’s hair.

Sometimes she’d go to his studio after work, bringing takeout—braised pork ribs from the restaurant his grandfather used to frequent, stir-fried greens from the market. She’d sit on the floor and watch him work, his brow furrowed as he adjusted a tiny screw with a pair of tweezers. "You’re very focused," she’d say, and he’d look up, his eyes softening. "Hard not to be when you’re here."

One weekend, he took her to the old town by the river. They walked along the stone streets, stopping at a tailor’s shop where his grandmother had bought clothes, a tea house where his grandfather had played chess. "I used to come here every summer when I was a kid," he said. "My grandma would give me five yuan to buy sugar-fried chestnuts, and I’d sit on the bridge and watch the boats go by."

They bought chestnuts from a street vendor, still warm in a paper bag, and sat on the bridge. The river glinted in the sunlight, and a group of children chased each other along the bank, laughing. Lin Mian leaned her head on his shoulder, and he wrapped his arm around her. "You know," he said, "my grandpa used to say that the best things in life are the ones that take time—fixing a camera, brewing good tea, loving someone."

Lin Mian squeezed his hand. "My mom used to say the same thing. She said love is like a watercolor painting. You start with light strokes, and then you build it up, layer by layer, until it’s something beautiful."

That night, they went back to his studio. He put on a record—"When I Fall in Love" by Nat King Cole—and pulled her close. They danced slowly, the phonograph’s melody mixing with the sound of the wind outside. Lin Mian closed her eyes, breathing in the scent of his soap and the faint smell of camera oil. For a moment, she forgot about the empty house, about the accident, about all the days she’d spent feeling like a part of her was missing. All she could feel was his hand on her back, his heartbeat against her chest, the warmth of his breath on her forehead.

Winter came, and with it, the anniversary of her parents’ death. Lin Mian woke up that morning with a heavy heart, the kind that made even getting out of bed feel like a chore. She stared at the ceiling for a long time, then got up and put on the sweater her mom had knitted for her—soft wool, light blue, a little too small now but still warm.

She was making coffee when the doorbell rang. It was Jiang Chen, holding a bouquet of white chrysanthemums and a paper bag. "I asked the shopkeeper about the best flowers for remembrance," he said, handing her the bouquet. "He said these are for people you love who are gone."

Lin Mian’s throat tightened. She’d never told him the exact date—she’d only mentioned that the anniversary was in December. He must have remembered, must have asked her neighbors or the school secretary. She stepped aside to let him in, and he put the flowers in a vase on the dining table, next to the photo of her parents.

"I made congee," he said, opening the paper bag. "My grandma used to make it when someone was sad. It’s plain, but it’s warm."

They sat at the table and ate congee slowly. Lin Mian told him about the last day she’d spent with her parents—they’d gone to the zoo, her dad had bought her a cotton candy that stained her fingers pink, her mom had taken a photo of her laughing with a giraffe. "I thought we’d have so many more days like that," she said, her voice breaking. "I was mad at them for a long time. For leaving me."

Jiang Chen took her hand, his thumb brushing over her knuckles. "It’s okay to be mad," he said. "Grief isn’t neat. My grandpa died when I was 16. I didn’t talk to anyone for a month. She told her parents about Jiang Chen—about his studio, his love for old cameras, the way he made her laugh when she was sad. "I think you’d like him," she said, brushing a leaf off the headstone. Lin Mian smiled. "My dad used to say that too. He said snow is nature’s way of saying ‘let’s try again.’"

He pulled out a small box, and when Lin Mian opened it, she gasped.

"My grandma had a locket like this," he said. "She kept a photo of my grandpa in it. I wanted you to have something to keep the people you love close."

Lin Mian put the locket around her neck. It was warm against her skin, like a hug. She leaned over and kissed him, soft at first, then deeper. When she pulled away, he was smiling, his eyes shining. "I love you," he said, quiet but sure. "I’ve loved you since the day we both reached for that phonograph."

"I love you too," she said. And for the first time, the words didn’t feel scary. They felt like coming home.

The children from her class were hiding behind a tree, and when she said yes, they ran out, cheering, holding up signs that said "Mr. Jiang, marry our teacher!" Xiao Yu gave her a drawing of a cat wearing a wedding veil, and Jiang Chen laughed until his eyes watered.

They got married in the autumn, in the school’s backyard, where the maple trees were red and gold. Lin Mian wore a white dress, and Jiang Chen wore a suit that fit him perfectly—tailored by the same tailor his grandmother had used. The phonograph played "The Moon Represents My Heart" as she walked down the aisle, her dad’s old watch on her wrist, the locket around her neck. Her students sat in the front row, waving paper flowers they’d made themselves. The shopkeeper from the old bookstore was there, and the vendor who sold sugar-fried chestnuts, and Jiang Chen’s aunt, who’d traveled all the way from Beijing.

He froze for a moment, then picked her up and spun her around, laughing so hard he almost knocked over the stack of records. That night, he took a polaroid of her hand resting on her stomach, and they put it in the locket next to the photo of her painting by the river.

One afternoon, when Xiao Yue was three, she climbed onto a chair and reached for the phonograph, her tiny fingers brushing the brass horn. "Daddy, what’s this?" she asked, looking up at Jiang Chen with wide eyes.

She thought about her parents, about Jiang Chen’s grandpa, about all the love that had been passed down from one generation to the next.

Jiang Chen looked up and saw her, and he smiled. He held out his hand, and she walked over, sitting down next to him. Xiao Yue climbed into her lap, wrapping her arms around her neck. "Mommy, sing!" she said, pointing at the phonograph.

Lin Mian started singing, her voice soft and clear. Jiang Chen joined in, and Xiao Yue babbled along, her tiny voice mixing with theirs. The phonograph played on, the needle moving slowly across the record, the melody filling the room with warmth.

Inside, there was love—warm, steady, enduring—like the scratchy music from the old phonograph, like the watercolor paintings on the walls, like the handprints of a little girl on the windowsill. It was the kind of love that takes time, that builds layer by layer, that stays even when the days are hard. It was the kind of love that makes a house a home, that makes a life feel full.

Lin Mian looked at Jiang Chen, at Xiao Yue, at the old phonograph playing its song. And she knew, with a certainty that filled her chest, that this was what happiness looked like.

Lin Mian put the locket around her neck. It was warm against her skin, like a hug. She leaned over and kissed him, soft at first, then deeper. When she pulled away, he was smiling, his eyes shining. "I love you," he said, quiet but sure. "I’ve loved you since the day we both reached for that phonograph."

"I love you too," she said. And for the first time, the words didn’t feel scary. They felt like coming home.

Spring came, and the old bookstore on Xingfu Road closed down. The shopkeeper gave Jiang Chen the phonograph as a gift, saying, "It’s better with someone who loves it." They moved it to Lin Mian’s house, placing it in the living room by the window, where the sunlight hit it just right.

Jiang Chen proposed that summer, on the bridge by the old town. He got down on one knee, holding a ring with a small diamond—"my grandma’s," he said—and asked her to marry him. The children from her class were hiding behind a tree, and when she said yes, they ran out, cheering, holding up signs that said "Mr. Jiang, marry our teacher!" Xiao Yu gave her a drawing of a cat wearing a wedding veil, and Jiang Chen laughed until his eyes watered.

They got married in the autumn, in the school’s backyard, where the maple trees were red and gold. Lin Mian wore a white dress, and Jiang Chen wore a suit that fit him perfectly—tailored by the same tailor his grandmother had used. The phonograph played "The Moon Represents My Heart" as she walked down the aisle, her dad’s old watch on her wrist, the locket around her neck. Her students sat in the front row, waving paper flowers they’d made themselves. The shopkeeper from the old bookstore was there, and the vendor who sold sugar-fried chestnuts, and Jiang Chen’s aunt, who’d traveled all the way from Beijing.

Lin Mian started singing, her voice soft and clear. Jiang Chen joined in, and Xiao Yue babbled along, her tiny voice mixing with theirs. The phonograph played on, the needle moving slowly across the record, the melody filling the room with warmth.

Inside, there was love—warm, steady, enduring—like the scratchy music from the old phonograph, like the watercolor paintings on the walls, like the handprints of a little girl on the windowsill. Lin Mian looked at Jiang Chen, at Xiao Yue, at the old phonograph playing its song. And she knew, with a certainty that filled her chest, that this was what happiness looked like.

Then the needle dropped, a faint scrape against vinyl that made Lin Mian’s breath hitch, and a scratchy melody spilled out—Chen Yixun’s "Red Rose." It hit her like a wave breaking over a quiet shore; that was the exact song playing on the kitchen radio the morning her parents dragged their suitcases out the door, laughing as her mother tucked a strand of hair behind her ear and promised to bring back a silk scarf from Suzhou. She’d stood in the doorway, clutching her favorite teddy bear, watching their car vanish around the maple tree at the end of the lane, never guessing it would be the last time she’d see their smiles.

Her breath caught in her throat, and she reached out unconsciously to touch the cold metal needle, its tip glinting like a tiny diamond under the shop’s dim incandescent bulb. Just as her fingertip brushed the tiny lever that controlled the arm, it collided with another hand. Warm, calloused from turning camera knobs and tightening screws, with a faint silvery scar along the knuckle—like a line drawn by a careless needle during a childhood mishap. Lin Mian jerked back as if burned, her cheeks flushing pink as the cherry blossoms that fell in spring, and when she looked up, she met a pair of amber eyes, crinkled at the corners like someone who smiled often, even when alone with a stack of old records. His lashes were thick, casting soft shadows in the low light, and there was a hint of amusement in his gaze—not at her awkwardness, but at the way their hands had tangled so naturally, as if they’d been reaching for the same thing all along.

"Sorry," the man said, pulling his hand back slightly—not in retreat, but in the quiet courtesy of someone who respected personal space. He was wearing a well-worn denim jacket, the cuffs rolled up to reveal a faded blue watch with a cracked glass face; its hands still ticked steadily, though the numbers were half-rubbed off, a testament to years of reliable service. "I’ve been coming to check on this thing for a month. The old man here says it’s a 1992 model, from a family that moved abroad to Canada. Works like a charm if you’re gentle with the needle—she’s a bit temperamental, like an old lady who doesn’t suffer fools." He nodded at the phonograph, his tone fond, as if speaking of an old friend who’d shared countless mornings and evenings with him. "I almost missed it last week—he was gonna sell it to a collector from Shanghai, but I begged him to hold on. Told him it wasn’t just a machine to me."

The man glanced at the rain streaking the fogged windows, then back at her, his gaze lingering on the way she hugged her arms around her chest, as if trying to ward off a chill that wasn’t just from the weather, but from the empty spaces in her life.

He tilted his chin toward the small counter by the door, where a chipped enamel kettle whistled softly, sending a wisp of steam curling toward the ceiling like a lazy question. "The shopkeeper makes it with real milk and a pinch of cinnamon—tastes like my grandma’s, back when she still had all her teeth and could bake osmanthus cakes that filled the whole alley with sweetness. "Wooden shelves lined with resistors and capacitors, a faded poster of Teresa Teng on the wall, and this exact phonograph by the door. I made him a band-aid out of construction paper and glitter—pink, his least favorite color—and he wore it to work every day that week. His coworkers teased him, but he just said it was his ‘lucky charm.’" Her voice softened, and she smiled at the memory, the first genuine one that hadn’t tasted like sadness in weeks.

Jiang Chen laughed, a warm sound that made the cold shop feel brighter. "My grandpa once tried to fix a record player with a rubber band. It played ‘Moon River’ at double speed for a week. We couldn’t stop laughing whenever it came on."

When she left, it was dark outside. Jiang Chen walked her down the stairs, and at the door, he said, "I made something for you." He handed her a small envelope. Inside was a polaroid photo—of the phonograph, with the sunset streaming through the skylight behind it. On the back, he’d written: "For the girl who loves watercolors and old songs."

Lin Mian taped the photo to the fridge that night. Next to it was a photo of her parents, taken at the Great Wall when she was ten. For the first time in months, she didn’t feel like the house was too big, too quiet.

They started seeing each other regularly. Sometimes he’d come to her school during recess, bringing steamed buns from the shop down the street. The kids would crowd around him, asking about his cameras, and he’d let them hold the small point-and-shoots he kept in his bag. "Mr. Jiang is cooler than Spider-Man," Xiao Yu told Lin Mian one day, loud enough for Jiang Chen to hear. He laughed and ruffled the boy’s hair.

Sometimes she’d go to his studio after work, bringing takeout—braised pork ribs from the restaurant his grandfather used to frequent, stir-fried greens from the market. She’d sit on the floor and watch him work, his brow furrowed as he adjusted a tiny screw with a pair of tweezers. "You’re very focused," she’d say, and he’d look up, his eyes softening. "Hard not to be when you’re here."

One weekend, he took her to the old town by the river. They walked along the stone streets, stopping at a tailor’s shop where his grandmother had bought clothes, a tea house where his grandfather had played chess. "I used to come here every summer when I was a kid," he said. "My grandma would give me five yuan to buy sugar-fried chestnuts, and I’d sit on the bridge and watch the boats go by."

They bought chestnuts from a street vendor, still warm in a paper bag, and sat on the bridge. The river glinted in the sunlight, and a group of children chased each other along the bank, laughing. Lin Mian leaned her head on his shoulder, and he wrapped his arm around her. "You know," he said, "my grandpa used to say that the best things in life are the ones that take time—fixing a camera, brewing good tea, loving someone."

Lin Mian squeezed his hand. "My mom used to say the same thing. She said love is like a watercolor painting. You start with light strokes, and then you build it up, layer by layer, until it’s something beautiful."

That night, they went back to his studio. He put on a record—"When I Fall in Love" by Nat King Cole—and pulled her close. They danced slowly, the phonograph’s melody mixing with the sound of the wind outside. Lin Mian closed her eyes, breathing in the scent of his soap and the faint smell of camera oil. For a moment, she forgot about the empty house, about the accident, about all the days she’d spent feeling like a part of her was missing. All she could feel was his hand on her back, his heartbeat against her chest, the warmth of his breath on her forehead.

She stared at the ceiling for a long time, then got up and put on the sweater her mom had knitted for her—soft wool, light blue, a little too small now but still warm.

She stepped aside to let him in, and he put the flowers in a vase on the dining table, next to the photo of her parents.

She’d stood in the doorway, clutching her favorite teddy bear, watching their car vanish around the maple tree at the end of the lane, never guessing it would be the last time she’d see their smiles.

Her breath caught in her throat, and she reached out unconsciously to touch the cold metal needle, its tip glinting like a tiny diamond under the shop’s dim incandescent bulb. Just as her fingertip brushed the tiny lever that controlled the arm, it collided with another hand. Warm, calloused from turning camera knobs and tightening screws, with a faint silvery scar along the knuckle—like a line drawn by a careless needle during a childhood mishap. Lin Mian jerked back as if burned, her cheeks flushing pink as the cherry blossoms that fell in spring, and when she looked up, she met a pair of amber eyes, crinkled at the corners like someone who smiled often, even when alone with a stack of old records. His lashes were thick, casting soft shadows in the low light, and there was a hint of amusement in his gaze—not at her awkwardness, but at the way their hands had tangled so naturally, as if they’d been reaching for the same thing all along.

"Sorry," the man said, pulling his hand back slightly—not in retreat, but in the quiet courtesy of someone who respected personal space. He was wearing a well-worn denim jacket, the cuffs rolled up to reveal a faded blue watch with a cracked glass face; its hands still ticked steadily, though the numbers were half-rubbed off, a testament to years of reliable service. "I’ve been coming to check on this thing for a month. The old man here says it’s a 1992 model, from a family that moved abroad to Canada. Works like a charm if you’re gentle with the needle—she’s a bit temperamental, like an old lady who doesn’t suffer fools." He nodded at the phonograph, his tone fond, as if speaking of an old friend who’d shared countless mornings and evenings with him. Lin Mian nodded, her throat suddenly dry as cotton left in the sun. She didn’t mention the empty house she’d moved back into after the accident, the way she still set three bowls at dinner sometimes (reaching for a third pair of chopsticks before the cold weight of loss settled in), or how she’d started sleeping with her mom’s old sweater tucked under her pillow. But when Jiang Chen talked about his grandfather’s hands—gnarled from years of twisting screws, but steady enough to thread a wire through a tiny hole—the words spilled out, unplanned and raw. I made him a band-aid out of construction paper and glitter—pink, his least favorite color—and he wore it to work every day that week. Jiang Chen laughed, a warm sound that made the cold shop feel brighter. "My grandpa once tried to fix a record player with a rubber band. It played ‘Moon River’ at double speed for a week. We couldn’t stop laughing whenever it came on."

The rain stopped at dusk. Jiang Chen walked her to the bus stop, and before she got on, he said, "I’m gonna buy that phonograph tomorrow. If you want… you could come over sometime. I’ve got a stack of old records my grandpa left me. Teresa Teng, Zhou Xuan, even some old jazz."

Lin Mian nodded before she could overthink it. She wrote her phone number on a scrap of paper from her sketchbook—there was a tiny watercolor of a cat in the corner—and handed it to him. His fingers brushed hers again, and this time, she didn’t pull away.

Jiang Chen’s studio was on the third floor of an old brick building, with a skylight that let in soft light during the day. The walls were lined with shelves holding cameras of every shape and size—boxy Polaroids from the 80s, sleek rangefinders from the 60s, a wooden view camera that looked like it belonged in a museum. Lin Mian ran her finger along the spines. She stopped at a yellowed sleeve with a black-and-white photo of a woman in a cheongsam, holding a microphone. "Teresa Teng?"

She told him about her students—Xiao Yu, who drew cats on every worksheet; Xiao Hong, who was afraid of watercolors but loved oil pastels; the time the whole class had painted a mural of the city’s old streets on the school wall.

Inside was a polaroid photo—of the phonograph, with the sunset streaming through the skylight behind it. On the back, he’d written: "For the girl who loves watercolors and old songs."
